Endorsement: California isn’t a lab rat. Prop 40 treats us like one
There’s no denying the visceral satisfaction of a billionaire bloodletting. But will the measure’s wealth tax actually help the state?
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Updated Oct 31, 2026 1:42 p.m.
Taxation, like everything else in life, is an exercise in trade-offs.
How much public good can a tax extract before it passes the tipping point into harm?
As it relates to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/prop-40-41-42-california-22476000.php) on California’s November ballot, many believe you don’t have to look very hard to find where the cost-benefit needle falls.
The measure would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on anyone whose total net worth is greater than $1 billion as of Dec. 31, 2026, and who was a California resident on Jan. 1, 2026. After administrative costs, 90% of the revenue would go to public healthcare, while the other 10% would go to food assistance and education. The total collected could range from $28 billion to $100 billion — depending on whose math you believe. (California’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates the state will “probably” (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) collect “tens of billions.”)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Whatever the total, there’s no denying that California billionaires — who by some counts control a combined $2 trillion (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) in wealth — can afford to shoulder it.
Darien Shanske, a UC Davis law professor and a coauthor of Prop 40, called the measure a “rounding error” on the fortunes of California’s wealthiest.
For this mostly bloodless toll, Californians get relief from President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful” Medicaid cuts and radiate with satisfaction at sending a landmark message about wealth inequality.
Or so it would seem.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Is Prop 40 so flawlessly executed that California has nothing to lose if it passes?
Opposition from the California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood, California Medical Association, the NAACP, California Professional Firefighters and the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California suggests not.
Let’s start with the healthcare organizations, which would effectively receive 90% of Prop 40’s funds. Why are they opposed?
Dustin Corcoran, CEO of the California Medical Association, said in an endorsement interview that there’s no guarantee Prop 40’s payload will arrive in time to backfill Trump’s cuts. The state has no existing system for assessing billionaire wealth, he said, and it will likely take years to develop one.
Corcoran cited his experience as a backer of Prop 56, which passed in 2016 and imposed a tax on vape products.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“It probably took the Franchise Tax Board 10 years of us beating them up because they couldn’t figure out how to get the tax right,” he said. “And that was a fairly straightforward thing to try and figure out.”
Even if the money does land, and that’s a big if, Corcoran argued that weak “anti-supplantation” protections in the measure will allow lawmakers to spend its revenue however they see fit — undermining one of Prop 40’s most powerful arguments, the urgency of the moment for healthcare.
University of Missouri School of Law Professor David Gamage, one of Prop 40’s coauthors, disputed these notions. He estimated that “75% of billionaire wealth is in publicly traded assets,” making much of it easy to track. And even if the measure does have supplantation holes, political pressure will prevent California politicians from treating Prop 40 revenue like a slush fund.
These vague assurances don’t persuade Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California. Healthcare organizations like hers, she said, use forward-looking budgets. They can’t commit to providing services if they can’t definitively rely on money coming in to pay for them.
Meanwhile, Prop 40 puts the money Hicks can count on in jeopardy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That’s because California’s budget is overly dependent on income taxes — roughly half of which (https://lao.ca.gov/LAOEconTax/Article/Detail/7)historically come from the ultra-wealthy top 1% of taxpayers.
Studying the impacts of Prop 40 “was an eye-opening experience for what California’s tax structure is and how the wealthy are a part of it,” Hicks said.
This gets at the real questions surrounding Prop 40 and why so many otherwise progressive organizations oppose the tax: Will billionaires leave the state if the measure passes, and will they take their companies with them?
“Good riddance” is the popular retort among online commentators.
But that attitude is childish and self-defeating. A recent case study explained why.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The world’s wealthiest man, Elon Musk, left California in 2020, citing high taxes as one of his reasons. He took Tesla’s corporate headquarters with him to Texas the following year.
By some estimates, California lost an estimated $2.5 billion (https://www.businessinsider.com/why-did-elon-musk-move-texas-wealth-tax-capital-gains-2021-11) in capital gains revenue from one stock transaction in the first year of Musk’s move. In a state where 40% of state dollars are required by law to go to public education, that’s a $1 billion hole in California’s school budget from one man alone.
This answers why the formidable California Teachers Association — never one to shy away from a back-alley tax brawl — doesn’t support Prop 40.
Then there are the jobs.
Many Tesla workers stayed behind in California. But new Tesla jobs are now sprouting up across Texas, including nearly 10,000 for a proposed $10 billion solar cell factory (https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/09/18/teslas-10-1-billion-texas-solar-gigafactory-clears-key-tax-hurdle/).
You’ve heard the aphorism, “Keep your friends close and your enemies closer.” Here’s a real-world example of why.
Sending billionaires and the jobs and economic might that come with them to Texas or Florida does not help California. Nor does it help the prospects for building a more just society. It simply makes those red states more powerful.
So, will Prop 40 send billionaires fleeing?
A working paper from Stanford says yes, (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35899) and argues that exodus will result in a net tax revenue loss of nearly $39 billion for California (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/billionaire-tax-analysis-22485993.php). Indeed, some billionaires — most famously Google cofounder Sergey Brin, who has dumped hundreds of millions into opposing Prop 40 — have already announced their departures.
Some economists dispute the Stanford study (https://x.com/gabriel_zucman/status/2112988796082176375), arguing it ignores basic human motivation. Prop 40 will hit any billionaire who lived in California as of Jan. 1. Why would they uproot their lives now over a one-time tax they have to pay regardless — especially one they can easily afford?
We’d counter that California’s nation-leading 13.3% marginal income tax rate — necessary as it may be (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php), given our state’s finances — already poses a flight risk. Even Gamage said he was “uncomfortable” (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) with the top rate. A wealth tax merely compounds a danger that already exists.
It’s true that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has committed to ponying up (https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/billionaires-fight-tax-hike-jensen-160907521.html) his estimated $8 billion in dues. And Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has apparently agreed to stay in California for eight years after strong-arming the company (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/billionaire-tax-analysis-22485993.php#:~:text=Meta%20revealed%20in%20a%20Securities%20and%20Exchange%20Commission%20filing%20that%20Mark%20Zuckerberg%20was%20considering%20leaving%20California%2C%20but%20agreed%20to%20stay%20after%20the%20company%20gave%20him%20a%20new%20stock%20deal) into eating his wealth tax burden.
Yet the debate around flight risk has largely focused on the wealthiest of the wealthy. Less discussed are the paper billionaires — those with unrealized stakes in valuable startups and other private companies.
Prop 40’s method for assessing this wealth (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-17/mark-cuban-rips-ro-khannas-insane-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-plan) is dubious. Some believe the measure allows voting shares or control percentage to be used in calculating wealth, rather than ownership stake, which could be wildly off. The measure does offer a mechanism for the wealthy to contest their asset valuations, but at what point are companies going to decide enough is enough and seek their fortunes elsewhere?
“Only idiot startup founders stay in Cali” if Prop 40 passes, billionaire investor Mark Cuban has said on social media. (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-17/mark-cuban-rips-ro-khannas-insane-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-plan?utm_source=chatgpt.com) “You can bet if I’m investing in a multi-billion-dollar startup, I’m asking them to move from California first.”
“Boo hoo,” you say?
California’s startup culture is a crucial engine of its economy. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, companies in the state receive nearly half of all American venture capital (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2024/4942/CalFacts-2024-120224.pdf). Another study found these investments help employ 1.2 million people (https://www.nvca.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/California-VC-State-Data.pdf). As companies grow their roots, California’s budget sees the benefit.
Many argue that the talent ecosystem in California makes an exodus impossible.
But people said the same thing about Hollywood for decades. Now the entertainment industry is shedding thousands of jobs to states like Georgia and North Carolina that offer more favorable economic incentives.
If movie titans are willing to abandon a company town practically built to indulge their excess, it’s not a stretch to imagine a significant portion of the tech universe fleeing to Miami or Austin, where workforce housing is cheaper, they would pay no state income tax, and the sword of future wealth taxes would no longer hang over their endeavors.
All this speaks to why tackling extreme wealth is better approached at the federal level. There’s evidence from Spain and elsewhere that the wealthy will shop around regionally (https://direct.mit.edu/rest/article-abstract/101/2/214/58521/Relocation-of-the-Rich-Migration-in-Response-to) for lower taxes. There’s much less evidence that they’ll flee the country.
We are already seeing momentum for a federal inequality crackdown. Democrats are poised to retake Congress, and Rep. Laura Friedman, D-Burbank, recently announced legislation that would impose an excise tax of 23.8% (https://news.bgov.com/bloomberg-government-news/house-democrat-pitches-new-wealth-tax-as-midterms-draw-near) on most line-of-credit loans — which are leveraged against assets like stocks — above $1 million.
Ever wonder how the Zuckerbergs of the world get by on a salary of $1? Borrowing against stock gives them access to cash without having to pay capital gains. In fact, in some cases, interest payments on these loans are tax deductible under federal policy.
Fixing these loopholes would force the ultra-wealthy to either take salaries or liquidate assets when they need cash, which would mean income tax boons for states like California.
Obviously, with Trump still in charge, it could take a few years for these and other changes to manifest.
Instead of being patient, however, Prop 40 throws the full weight of risk on California’s shoulders now.
“Are we destined to live in an oligarchic society begging for crumbs while our economic and political lives are controlled by a handful of the wealthiest people on Earth?”
We wholeheartedly agree with these sentiments, espoused by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders at a recent rally in support of Prop 40.
But living up to them demands strategic thinking, not primal screaming.
Ultimately, neither this editorial board nor anyone else has any idea what the full effect of Prop 40 will be.
Even Emmanuel Saez, the French economist and an author of Prop 40, has conceded that his measure is an “experiment.” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tLQFHYqkVtY)
It just happens to be one dropped into the maw of the world’s fourth-largest economy — a wealthy state in aggregate, but one with a volatile, incoherent system of taxation (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-43-ballot-california-22477053.php) and the highest poverty rate in the nation.
If Prop 40 backfires, California will have chased away its cash cows with no backup plan. Our sales and income taxes are already the highest in the nation; there’s no more room for hikes. Meanwhile, Prop 13 stunts our ability to raise new revenue from property taxes.
No one is coming to save us. And it won’t be the wealthy who suffer.
Maybe, just maybe, the stakes are too high in California to be playing a game of chicken. Maybe the brightest and boldest minds in the field of economic justice should help stabilize California’s tax base before turning our state into a laboratory?

PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. It’s time to make billionaires pay their fair share and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
CON
Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can’t afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. No safeguards, no accountability. Join California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children’s Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Democrats and Republicans: NO on 40.

## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires.*** Under Proposition 40, billionaires who were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to 5 percent of their net worth.
The tax would be due in 2027.
Taxpayers would have the option to spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so.
Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
***Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care.*** The state would decide how and when to spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services.
Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public.
The rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax.
Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.

Proposition 40
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
Analysis of Measure
Background
California Is Home to Many Billionaires. Several of the wealthiest people in the world live in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person's wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person's net worth is the value of all the things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology companies.
Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending. The state and federal government spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is for Medi-Cal, the state's health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.
Proposal
Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires. Under Proposition 40, billionaires who were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to 5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care. The state would decide how and when to spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services. Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax. Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.
Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 41 or 42 on this same ballot receive more "yes" votes than Proposition 40, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 41 or 42 conflict with Proposition 40.
Fiscal Effects
Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax. The state probably would collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock prices, which are always changing.
Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues. California billionaires, like all those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than $1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state's General Fund, which is the account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.
State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax. The state would have costs to determine how much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Temporary state revenue increase from a new wealth tax on billionaires. These wealth tax revenues probably would add up to tens of billions of dollars spread over several years.
Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue collected from billionaires.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires.

PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 40
YES ON PROP. 40 TO TAX BILLIONAIRES
Trump’s “Big, Ugly Bill” slashed funding for healthcare in California to pay for more billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. Vote YES on Prop. 40 to make billionaires finally pay their fair share in taxes and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
FUND HEALTHCARE, NOT BILLIONAIRE TAX BREAKS
Prop. 40 makes approximately 200 California billionaires pay a modest, one-time tax on their global wealth to keep local hospitals and ERs open and healthcare affordable for millions of Californians.
It will raise about $100 billion to replace the funding Trump and his billionaire donors took from working people to line their pockets. The funds will go to life-saving medical care for seniors, veterans, and families. It will allow millions of Californians to keep their health insurance and not see their premiums skyrocket. It will prevent mass teacher layoffs in our public schools and keep children fed through food assistance programs.
BILLIONAIRES SHOULD PAY THEIR FAIR SHARE
You pay your taxes out of every paycheck, but billionaires pay much lower rates than working families. They insist on paying less, even as they get bigger and bigger tax breaks.
Prop. 40 enacts a one-time tax paid ONLY by Californians worth more than $1 billion, a small group of people who together hold $2 trillion in wealth-most of which will never be taxed due to loopholes that favor the ultra-wealthy.
Billionaires amassed their extreme wealth on the backs of the middle class, and we have a chance to make them pay their fair share so WE aren’t stuck paying more for healthcare.
BERNIE SANDERS SUPPORTS PROP. 40
U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders strongly supports voting YES on Prop. 40, even if some politicians in Sacramento are protecting billionaires over working people.
“The idea that [billionaires] are saying it’s ok for children to die, for people not to get the healthcare they need, that they’re going to punish the people of California-it’s outrageous.”
-U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders.
DON’T BELIEVE THE BILLIONAIRES’ LIES
A small group of morally bankrupt billionaires is spreading lies about Prop. 40, because they want working people to foot the bill for their tax breaks.
Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin’s wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to oppose Prop. 40. He’d rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay his fair share in taxes.
Billionaires like Brin have bought and paid for some corrupt politicians and organizational leaders to also oppose Prop. 40-but actual teachers, Planned Parenthood workers, nurses, and union members support it. Those opposing Prop. 40 have not put forth any viable solution to replacing the funding Trump took from us.
Of course these billionaires and their puppets don’t want a billionaire tax, but you should-because someone has to pay, and working people are already paying enough for healthcare.
SAVE LIVES. TAX BILLIONAIRES.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
Victoria Barron , Patient Access Specialist
Planned Parenthood of Pacific Southwest
Denise Robb , Ph.D., Member of American Federation of Teachers
Local 1521
Los Angeles College Faculty Guild
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 40
CALIFORNIA’S EDUCATION, HEALTHCARE, PUBLIC SAFETY, LABOR AND BUSINESS LEADERS ALL OPPOSE PROP. 40’s FLAWED TAX SCHEME
Prop. 40 is a flawed tax scheme that will damage our state while taxpayers pay the price.
Here’s why a broad coalition of California teachers, doctors, clinics, hospitals, firefighters, taxpayers, blue-collar labor unions, businesses, Democrats and Republicans oppose 40:
Prop. 40 won’t fill any funding gap-IT WILL COST CALIFORNIA $25 BILLION in lost revenue for schools, healthcare and public safety.
Prop. 40 won’t fix healthcare or lower costs for consumers-it’s a blank check that ALLOWS THE LEGISLATURE TO GIVE BILLIONS TO HEALTH INSURANCE COMPANIES, with no guarantees struggling families see a single cent to help them with high healthcare costs.
Prop. 40 won’t help schools: it exempts itself from California’s voter-approved protections for school funding. That SHORTCHANGES PUBLIC SCHOOLS $3 BILLION ANNUALLY.
Prop. 40 doesn’t solve inequality in California. It just pushes out the companies and successful residents who drive California’s economy, jobs and tax base-FORCING OTHER TAXPAYERS TO MAKE UP THE DIFFERENCE.
There’s more: the French economists and the lone group behind Prop. 40 knew the money from their flawed one-time tax would run out, so they included a loophole that lets the Legislature expand the tax without a vote of the people.
Prop. 40 has no accountability or oversight, and no safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended.
California needs stable, accountable revenue to fund our schools, healthcare and public safety-NOT PROP. 40.
Get the facts and vote no on Prop. 40.
April O’Connor , Teacher
California Teachers Association
Rob Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association (CalTax)
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 40
No on 40-FLAWED WEALTH TAX “EXPERIMENT” HURTS ALL CALIFORNIANS
Prop. 40 is a poorly designed tax scheme that will damage our economy and cost our state budget billions of dollars-without doing anything to lower healthcare costs for Californians.
This measure is a one-time tax that only provides temporary funds. When the money runs out, the politicians will be back with yet another tax.
PROP. 40 WILL COST CALIFORNIA $25 BILLION IN LOST REVENUE FOR HEALTHCARE, EDUCATION
A study by Stanford University economists found the tax will cost California $25 billion as the tax drives companies and wealthy residents out-of-state.
These residents create new businesses, drive our economic growth and already pay nearly half the income taxes that fund state programs. If they leave, it will create a huge hole in our budget, threatening core services like education, healthcare and public safety or forcing other taxpayers to make up the difference.
California’s DOCTORS, HOSPITALS AND CLINICS OPPOSE PROP. 40 because the lost funding will endanger patients’ access to healthcare. “Prop. 40 doesn’t help the need for stable healthcare funding.
Prop. 40 makes it worse.”-Jodi Hicks, President and CEO, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California
PROP. 40 IS WRITTEN TO GIVE POLITICIANS NEW POWER TO EXPAND THE TAX
Prop. 40 isn’t just a “billionaire tax.” The special interests behind the measure wrote it to give the State Legislature power to amend the measure-without voter approval.
Independent legal analysis found Prop. 40 opens the door to expanding the tax to the assets of ALL Californians-to your savings, home equity and even retirement funds. www.ReadltForYourself.org
PROP. 40 TAXES RETIREMENT ACCOUNTS FOR THE FIRST TIME
Prop. 40 would be the first in California history to tax retirement accounts-a dangerous precedent. If it passes, it will inevitably be expanded to tax more Californians’ retirement savings.
PROP. 40 IS A RECIPE FOR MORE WASTEFUL SPENDING
State government spending is up 79% since 2019, without delivering better results on key issues like crime, housing and homelessness. But Prop. 40 includes no accountability, transparency or oversight provisions to ensure funds are spent as intended.
Instead, Prop. 40: • Exempts itself from voter-approved constitutional protections for schools, shortchanging classrooms over $3 billion annually. www.ProtectCaliforniaSchools.org • Exempts itself from the voter-approved state spending limit, including its requirement that excess revenues get returned to taxpayers. • Includes no safeguards to prevent billions from going directly to health insurance companies and CEOs.
AUTHORS ADMIT THE ONE-TIME TAX IS AN EXPERIMENT
The French economists who co-authored Prop. 40 have unsuccessfully proposed wealth taxes in France and the European Union that were rejected due to economic concerns. They call Prop. 40 “an experiment” that may backfire but say “California is the ideal place to test their idea.”
We shouldn’t risk California’s future on a costly economic experiment. www.WhoWroteProp40.org
PROP. 40 IS OPPOSED BY LABOR AND BUSINESS, DEMOCRATS AND REPUBLICANS, TEACHERS AND FIREFIGHTERS
Prop. 40 is opposed by Governor Gavin Newsom, the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, and the following organizations: California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, California Children’s Hospital Association, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, California Conference of Carpenters, California Professional Firefighters, California Asian Pacific Chamber of Commerce, California Council for Affordable Housing, California Taxpayers Association, California Chamber of Commerce, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
Join us and vote no on this flawed tax scheme.
Visit www.VoteNoOn40.org for more information.
René Bravo , M.D., President
California Medical Association
Francisco Silva , CEO
California Primary Care Association
Dr. Debra Schade , President
California School Boards Association
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 40
LET’S CHECK THE FACTS
1. Prop. 40 is a BILLIONAIRE tax. It cannot be applied to anyone else-working people already pay more than their fair share.
2. Prop. 40 will GENERATE $100 billion to replace the healthcare funding Trump cut to fund billionaire tax breaks.
3. Billionaires pay MUCH LOWER TAX RATES compared to what working families pay out of every paycheck. DON’T LISTEN TO BILLIONAIRE LIES
The billionaires who helped Trump pass the “Big, Beautiful Bill” have spent millions to trick you into voting against a billionaire tax.
Don’t be fooled. The endorsements and studies from the billionaires are hiding the truth-they’re pushing a Trump agenda that protects billionaires and hurts everyday taxpayers.
ACTUAL DOCTORS, NURSES, TEACHERS, AND WORKERS SUPPORT PROP. 40
While some organizational leaders and lobbyists have sided with billionaires, the working people they’re supposed to represent are standing behind Prop. 40 and urging you to vote YES. Supporters include:
California Nurses Association, Representative Ro Khanna, Doctors with the Committee of Interns and Residents, SEIU, California League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), Clergy and Laity United for Economic Justice (CLUE)
OPPONENTS OF PROP. 40 HAVE NO PLAN TO SAVE YOUR HEALTHCARE
The billionaires and their puppets have not put forth ANY viable solution to replacing the healthcare funding Trump took from us. They’d rather the middle class get stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs than pay their fair share.
Vote YES on Prop. 40.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
Victoria Barron , Patient Access Specialist
Planned Parenthood of Pacific Southwest

The Bottom Line (https://www.cnbc.com/global-cfo-council/) California's Proposition 40: What voters need to know about billionaire wealth tax battle
Published Thu, Oct 22 2026 8:05 AM EDT Updated Thu, Oct 22 2026 12:04 PM EDT
Trevor Laurence Jockims (https://www.cnbc.com/trevor-laurence-jockims/)
WATCH LIVE (https://www.cnbc.com/live-tv/)
Key Points
California's Proposition 40, the Nov. 3 Election Day ballot measure, would levy a one-time, 5% "wealth tax" on residents of the state with a net worth above $1 billion, an estimated 200-250 billionaire individuals.
While polling from just a few months ago showed a significant edge for the wealth tax, more recent polling suggests the gap has narrowed, and prediction markets expect defeat.
Proponents say the measure could raise as much as $100 billion to fund healthcare in the state after significant cuts resulting from President Trump's tax act, but fears of billionaires leaving the state, highlighted this week by Mark Zuckerberg's invoking of that threat to gain a new stock plan from Meta, are among reasons some economists expect a big government revenue hit.
Opponents include Gov. Gavin Newsom, both candidates to replace him, and Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who is among leaders of an effort to defeat the measure, with billionaire-aligned groups spending an estimated $1 million per day.

Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/arguments-rebuttals.htm), California's billionaire tax proposal, would authorize a one-time, 5% "wealth tax" (https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/10/21/what-to-know-about-the-billionaire-tax-on-the-ballot-in-california.html) on residents of the state with a net worth above $1 billion. The Nov. 3 Election Day ballot measure has divided politicians, the wealthy, economists, public policy groups, and voters, and it is looking more likely that the vote is headed down to the wire.
The initiative is a major test of the appetite for state-level taxation of extreme wealth — its result, economists say, could shape how other states approach wealth tax policy going forward.
What the latest polls show
In a University of California Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll conducted in September, 45% of likely voters said they would vote "Yes" on Proposition 40, while 42% said they would vote "No."
The results continued a recent shift (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-wealth-tax-polls-2026.html?eafs_enabled=false) in the pollster's data, with the "Yes" edge shrinking from 7% to 3%. In its early August survey, UC Berkeley IGS found 48% of likely voters said they would vote yes. In its polling last March, "Yes" on Prop 40 had a 19% margin, with 52% of those polled expressing support and only 33% expressing opposition. According to its September poll, 13% of voters remain undecided.
A more recent poll conducted by Mason-Dixon Polling & Research for NBC Universal and Telemundo found "Yes" still has a sizable 10% advantage.
Large partisan differences characterize support and opposition to Proposition 40, with Democrats supporting it by more than three to one, while Republicans are opposed nearly eight to one. The views
of non-partisan voters are similar to those of the overall electorate.
While "Yes" continues to have an edge in the polls, prediction markets see Prop 40 going down to defeat by a wide margin. Both Kalshi (https://kalshi.com/markets/kxcawealthtax/will-the-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-initiative-pass/kxcawealthtax-26) and Polymarket (https://polymarket.us/event/ref-ca-blntax-2026-11-03) have the odds of passage currently at under 30%. These markets are not structured with methodologies used by traditional political polling.
How much money the measure could raise
The vast majority of the tax revenue would be used on state-funded healthcare programs, which will help offset healthcare cuts stemming from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/05/08/tax-break-wealthy-investors-qsbs.html) signed into law by President Trump last year, and which is estimated by the state's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office to cost California "as much as tens of billions of dollars" though it says the impact on general funding will ultimately be determined by discretionary healthcare policy choices made by the legislature.
There are an estimated 200-250 billionaires (https://cabillionairetracker.org/) residing in California, based on tracking of Forbes data and other sources.
Alan Auerbach, economics professor at Berkeley, said the concentration of wealth among a very small number of Californians is a key sticking point of the proposal. On the estimates of around 200 individuals, he said, "Even among this number, wealth is very concentrated among the [very] wealthiest."

Squawk Box (https://www.cnbc.com/squawk-box-us/)
Proponents of the measure say it could raise roughly $100 billion (https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/galle-gamage-saez-shanskeCAbillionairetaxDec25.pdf) in new tax revenue, a figure that they say also accounts for 10% of tax avoidance and evasion.
The California Budget & Policy Center, a think tank focused on the needs of low- and middle-income citizens, describes the measure (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) as one that "could potentially raise tens of billions in revenue in the short-term to preserve critical services."
That echoes the view of the state Legislative Analyst's Office, which estimates (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) that the measure would raise "tens of billions of dollars," spread over a number of years.
The authors of a study from conservative-leaning Hoover Institution, including Stanford University finance professor Joshua Rauh, estimate $30 billion in new revenue (https://www.hoover.org/research/net-present-value-california-billionaire-tax-act), factoring in migration of billionaires out of the state and future constitutional challenges. But it is their outlook for longer-term economic harm, most recently updated in an NBER research paper (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35899) published this month, that has attracted the most attention among those battling over the measure.
Concerns about billionaires fleeing California
The idea of driving the super-wealthy (https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/10/21/campaign-against-billionaire-tax-heres-what-to-know.html) away from the state has become a major area of concern for the plan's critics, who argue that "mobility" fundamentally undermines the tax base. The estimates of tax revenue depend in part on whether billionaires are able to leave the state and avoid taxes, and how many billionaires decide to take this action.
Many have pointed to Google co-founder Sergey Brin's purchase of a Miami home in March 2026.
Auerbach acknowledged the roughly $100 billion revenue estimate advanced by supporters but cautioned that assumptions about mobility and behavioral change on the part of taxpayers are so broad in range that it is possible to arrive at revenue estimates that are "negative if one accounts for future losses in income taxes from people who will have left California."
The California Budget & Policy Center said the measure "may also lead to some income tax revenue losses in future years to the extent that billionaires leave the state to avoid the tax."
The state's nonpartisan fiscal advisor stated that there is a "possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue collected from billionaires."
The Hoover Institution forecasts that with billionaires contributing $3.3–$5.8 billion annually in state income taxes, "permanently lost income tax collections from departures more than offsets the one-time wealth tax revenue, yielding a net present value of negative $38.9 billion."
Andrew Gonzales, council representative, LA/OC Building and Construction Trades Council, speaks during a rally against Proposition 40 at the Iron Workers Apprenticeship Training Center on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026 in La Palma, CA.
Eric Thayer | Los Angeles Times | Getty Images
One of the most vocal critics comes within Democrats' own ranks, as incumbent California Governor Gavin Newsom has frequently argued that a state-level wealth tax could weaken California's long-term tax base.
"The fight to make the wealthiest Americans pay more in taxes is not one we should be fighting state by state," Newsom said in a June Substack post (https://gavinnewsom.substack.com/p/its-time-for-a-national-billionaires). "You may not be able to pick up and move to Texas or Florida to shelter your income from taxation, but I promise you that billionaires can, and do. Wealth is movable, and it shops for the state with the lowest taxes."
Newsom, who earlier this month officially said he was a No vote on Prop 40, while a Yes vote on another measure that would bar the state from considering retroactive taxes, has also argued that the proposal could ultimately reduce funding for public services if high earners leave the state, reducing investments in needs like teachers, librarians, childcare, firefighting and police.
Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor, said during a recent debate with Republican candidate Steve Hilton that "too many" California billionaires are not paying their fair share. He argued that when someone pays a lower tax rate than "a teacher, a firefighter, a nurse," they are not paying fairly. But Becerra said he will vote no on Proposition 40, because "this is not the way to do tax policy. ... What you don't do is, you don't have a policy where it's a one-time tax and it isn't predictable and sustainable," Becerra said.
"I agree that we can't drive more tax revenue out of our state, because we need that money here, and this initiative would do that," Hilton said.

The mobility question is critical when the wealth being targeted for taxation is concentrated in financial assets that can be moved, restructured, or shielded.
One of the proposal's drafters, Darien Shanske, a law professor at UC Davis, downplays reports of wealthy Californians relocating in anticipation of the measure. "This proposal was drafted by three law professors and includes a pathway for accelerated review for some issues because we are confident in the tax's design," he said. "Given the sledgehammer that the OBBBA took to services (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/01/21/trump-big-beautiful-bill-tax-breaks.html) in order to pay for unneeded regressive tax cuts, it makes sense to close the loophole at least temporarily," he added.
According to Shanske, under longstanding California residency law, many highly publicized relocations may not meaningfully alter tax exposure under the proposal. Any billionaire residing in the state on January 1, 2026 would still be taxed, he said, based on longstanding Californialaw (https://ota.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/54/2021/06/18010932_Bracamonte_Opinion_P.pdf). He also argues that many lawyers who represent the wealthy (https://news.bloombergtax.com/daily-tax-report-state/billionaires-fleeing-california-to-hit-tax-officials-scrutiny) say even billionaires who bought residences outside the state before that date may face hurdles in challenging state tax law.
Shanske say some relocation rhetoric is politically strategic: "I conclude they are loudly doing these silly things in order to defeat the measure by creating doubt and confusion," he said.
But the legal and constitutional challenges that could mount in the event of the ballot measure passing are issues of significant debate, and led to a social media dustup (https://x.com/gabriel_zucman/status/2112988785587925321?s=20) this week between backers of the proposal and the authors of the Hoover Institution research.
How wealth is valued
Some opposition to Prop. 40 centers as much around valuation complexity as the possibility of wealth flight.
Indeed, Prop. 40's scope of taxation applies to a mix of liquid and illiquid assets, including public equities, private business stakes, venture capital holdings, and complex ownership structures. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
"Valuing private companies and nontraded assets is an issue for any wealth tax," Auerbach said.
This issue is particularly relevant in California, where billionaire wealth is often tied to technology companies, startup equity and other illiquid assets whose valuations can fluctuate sharply and become contentious.
But Shanske says arguments that the proposal would prove administratively unworkable are unfounded.
"Most of the assets of billionaires are public and hence readily valued," Shanske said. "As for private companies, there is a default valuation formula based on the longstanding and successful formula used in Switzerland (https://kubera-equity.com/en/understanding-capitalization-rate-in-business-valuation/)," he said. "The tax can be deferred for 5 years (with a little interest) or deferred even longer if a taxpayer is truly illiquid."
Shanske says the most important point is that California's current tax structure largely fails to reach the wealthiest residents because billionaires often do not realize taxable income in the conventional sense.
"People at the very top do not pay much income tax because they do not earn much income, which is to say that, at the very top, California's progressive income tax is not progressive at all," Shanske said.
"The super wealthy do not earn much in salary, nor do they sell their assets and so they do not earn much in income. PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! The alternative presented by opponents: nothing. Newsom has no plan; the legislature is struggling with deficits.

**Billionaire flight:** Evidence is mixed. The design uses a retroactive-ish trigger (Jan 1, 2026 residency) so moving now doesn't help. Legal challenges exist but the drafters are top tax law scholars (Gamage, Galle, Shanske) plus Saez (Nobel-adjacent, Clark medal). The real-world debate: critics said it violates the constitutional limits on retroactive taxation; supporters argue California already taxes "clawback" for residents leaving. A one-time 5% levy on $2T of wealth (~$100B gross, ~$30-100B net depending on avoidance) is a substantial backfill for the Medi-Cal hole. The LAO's fiscal estimate is favorable: tens of billions in, less than $1B/year potentially out.

The main counterargument from serious economists (Hoover/Rauh): billionaires leave; income tax from billionaires ($3.3-5.8B/yr) could be lost; NPV negative. But the LAO (nonpartisan, the official source) estimates revenue loss "probably less than $1 billion per year." The one-time design reduces flight incentives because the tax is based on Jan 1, 2026 residency — moving in 2026-2027 doesn't avoid it. Future taxes would be needed for ongoing flight, but this is one-time.

Constitutionality: The retroactive element could face challenges under federal constitutional doctrines (e.g., Due Process for retroactive taxes, but retroactive taxes have been upheld — United States v. Carlton upheld a retroactive tax applied to transactions before enactment when rationally related). California courts have upheld exit taxes (the "clawback"). Also, courts could find Prop 41/42 conflicts. That's a risk but the drafters included expedited review.

The spending structure: 90% healthcare. Given the Medi-Cal cuts from OBBBA (estimated tens of billions over the decade), this is a targeted response. The state budget is in deficit; without new revenue, Medi-Cal cuts will harm millions.

Weighing: The LAO — the nonpartisan official analysis — says tens of billions in revenue with possible <$1B/year ongoing loss. That's a strongly positive net fiscal effect in the near term. The strongest criticisms (Hoover study, $25B loss, $3B/year school shortfall) come from conservative-leaning institutions or interested parties, and their assumptions about mass flight are contested (Young et al. 2016 "Millionaire Migration" found minimal flight; California's 2012 Prop 30 millionaire tax didn't cause the predicted exodus).

Also there's a governance/process argument: Props 41 and 42 are billionaire-funded counter-measures explicitly designed to nullify Prop 40. Voting Yes on 40 and No on 41/42 is coherent.

Ethically: billionaires' wealth grew enormously, effective tax rates at the very top are lower than middle class (true per Saez-Zucman research), federal government cut Medicaid to fund tax cuts for the wealthy. A one-time 5% levy on wealth over $1B (affecting ~200-250 people, excluding homes and retirement accounts) is a progressive, targeted response.

Risks: litigation, one-shot revenue, legislative discretion. But those are manageable relative to tens of billions for healthcare during a crisis.

ntion to the concentration of wealth in non-wage income.
What the wealthy are saying
In internal discussions, Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently said he might be forced to leave the state (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/technology/mark-zuckerberg-meta-california-wealth-tax.html?eafs_enabled=false) over the wealth tax, leading Meta's board to agree to insulate him from any financial and ownership impact by changing its stock structure, details revealed on Wednesday in an SEC filing (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1326801/000162828026066710/meta-20261021.htm). (The new class of shares will also provide Meta another source of capital for AI investments.)
Google co-founder Sergey Brin is among billionaires pouring money into an effort to defeat the measure, according to a recent Politico report (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/wealth-tax-sergey-brin-spending-01127374), spending "40 times what he put into politics in the previous two decades, making him the biggest individual donor to a ballot measure campaign in California history."
Groups supporting the "No" vote have contributed the largest sums to the battle over Proposition 40.
Building a Better California, whose top donors include Brin, has spent roughly $118 million (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/) on the campaign, according to the California Fair Political Practices Commission, and more on additional ballot measures designed to nullify Prop 40 if it is passed.
Service Employees International Union, the labor group leading support for the "Yes" campaign, has spent roughly $32 million.
But Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who oversees one of the two most valuable companies in the world (alongside Apple) and would be on the hook for as much as $8 billion in payments under the tax, has no issue with it. He recently told CBS Sunday Morning (https://x.com/CBSSunday/status/2112234190284435529?s=20) that it would be a "privilege" to pay the tax, consistent with views he has expressed (https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/01/07/nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-perfectly-fine-with-proposed-billionaire-tax.html) since the beginning of 2026 about the tax measure, and related to his views on the opportunities that the U.S. has offered him to succeed and grow his wealth.
Some within the CEO class have recently come out in favor of greater taxation on the wealthy, but not at the state level. United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby said in an interview with the New York Times (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/business/scott-kirby-united-airlines.html) this week that "We should have a national wealth tax — it won't work by state because people will just move. And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100 percent at some level. I would pay them."

Would it really be a one-time tax?
Uncertainty around whether the measure would remain strictly one-time could intensify those behavioral responses. "There is nothing in the proposition to keep the tax from being imposed again in the future, and recent history suggests it will be," Auerbach said.
While this sentiment rings true, there is a significant amount of precedent to suggest that not all tax hikes are created equal in the eyes of California voters.
Take, for example, Proposition 30, the 2012 California ballot measure that instilled "temporary taxes to fund education."
Prop. 30 imposed a temporary increase to the personal income tax for California residents making more than $250,000 annually, raising rates from anywhere between 1-3%, depending on total income, over the span of 7 years. Messaging surrounding the initiative was similar to that of this year's Prop. 40 – the tax increase would be a temporary remedial measure, necessary to preserve an essential state service, in its case, public education. Championed by Democratic leaders throughout the state, Prop. 30 went on to pass by a double-digit margin.
Ten years later, in 2022, a different Proposition 30 set to increase income taxes made the California ballot. This proposed "millionaire tax" would have raised income tax rates by 1.75% on earners with personal income greater than $2 million annually. The resulting revenue would have been used to fund programs to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, including investment in electric vehicles, charging stations, and firefighter training/recruitment. However, despite endorsements from many high-profile state figures and organizations, the "Yes on 30" campaign was never able to shake the label of a "special interest carveout (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2022/07/climate-change-california-newsom/)."
In the end, this Prop. 30 failed (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/11/california-election-results-prop30/) by a margin of over 15 percentage points statewide.
Shanske rejected the idea that the measure is designed as a stealth permanent tax increase.
"It is a one-time tax for a one-time emergency," he said. "Any further taxation would need to be voted on again."
Not only would it need to be voted on again, but the voters of California do regularly reject taxes, including on the wealthy, he said, citing not only Prop 30 but also 2020's Proposition 15 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_15,_Tax_on_Commercial_and_Industrial_Properties_for_Education_and_Local_Government_Funding_Initiative_(2020)).
Related ballot measures
Even if these practical and legal challenges are sidelined in the way Shanske suggests, Prop. 40 still faces the challenge of a potentially immediate repeal at the hands of a competing initiative on the very same ballot.
Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/), would bar the enactment of new and/or retroactive taxes on retirement holdings, personal assets, and individual savings after January 1, 2026. Given the proposed billionaire tax's structure, applying retroactively to billionaires living in the state as of January 1, 2026, Prop. 42 appears as a direct means of undercutting it.
Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/), meanwhile, would nullify any taxes adopted after Jan. 1, 2026 that would raise revenue breaching state spending limits, and require an independent state auditor to conduct recurring public audits of programs funded by new taxes. Proposition 40 includes a provision to allow the revenue to be allocated to healthcare and other social needs like food assistance even when spending limits are exceeded, an exemption from existing state law.
Gov. Newsom came out on Oct. 9 in support (https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/heres-gavin-newsom-voting-californias-172141607.html) of Proposition 42. He has yet to take a position on Proposition 41.
According to the state Legislative Analyst's Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026), "If Proposition 41 or 42 on this same ballot receive more "yes" votes than Proposition 40, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 41 or 42 conflict with Proposition 40."
Shanske says these proposals are "cynical deceptions" that would harm the state more than Prop 40.
Prop. 40's strongest backers, which include some of the state's largest and most influential healthcare unions, argue that, this time around, the message will be strong enough to propel the ambitious initiative over the finish line.
"Yes on 40 campaign is seeing an enormous wave of voters who believe that now is the moment to save healthcare for all Californians by taxing billionaires," said Debru Carthan, Vice President of SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, in a statement to CNBC.
Whether California voters echo this confidence remains to be seen. For supporters, the proposal represents an emergency fiscal response aimed at temporarily extracting revenue from unprecedented concentrations of wealth. For opponents, it represents a risky experiment that could weaken California's competitiveness and accelerate the mobility of capital, the wealthy, and entrepreneurs.

Billionaire Tax Explained: What Proposition 40 Would Mean for California
Implications of the One-Time Billionaire Wealth Tax for Californians
August 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Report
key takeaway
Prop. 40 would institute a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires to raise tens of billions in temporary revenue to address the loss of federal funding and other threats to health, nutrition, and education services, largely a result of H.R. 1 — the 2025 budget reconciliation law known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” Prop. 40 could potentially raise tens of billions in revenue in the short-term to preserve critical services, but may also lead to some income tax revenue losses in future years to the extent that billionaires leave the state to avoid the tax.

Prop. 40 Supporters and Opponents
Background
California, like many other states, is facing a number of challenges to its ability to meet the needs of its residents, including the impending impacts of the deep federal cuts to public health care and nutrition assistance (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/) and the rising costs of providing services due to inflation, an aging population with more complex needs, and the state’s ongoing housing crisis. The federal cuts to Medi-Cal alone are expected to cost the state tens of billions of dollars in lost funding and could lead to around 1.3 million Californians losing health care access by 2029-30. Meaningfully addressing these challenges will require California to raise a substantial amount of revenue (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/building-an-affordable-california-requires-public-investment/).
what is h.r. 1?
H.R. 1, the 2025 budget reconciliation law known (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/hr1-and-the-federal-budget-how-california-leaders-can-respond-to-trumps-cuts/) as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” signed by President Trump on July 4, 2025, will deeply harm Californians by cutting funding for essential health care and food assistance programs — while providing massive tax breaks to the wealthy and corporations. The spending cuts will disproportionately impact families with low incomes, immigrants, and communities of color, pushing more people into poverty and widening racial and economic inequities across the state.
Even prior to these more recent challenges, California was not generating enough revenue to meet the critical needs of all Californians through the state’s communities, evidenced by the state’s poverty rate remaining the highest in the nation (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-persistent-poverty-crisis-2024-rates-remain-alarmingly-high/). In addition to the human suffering caused by failing to ensure Californians can regularly access health care, put enough food on the table, and meet their other basic needs, such a failure dampens the state economy by preventing some individuals from fully participating in it and puts fiscal pressures on state and local governments as more households are forced to turn to costly emergency services and systems of last resort.
In the near term, Prop. 40 would likely generate tens of billions in revenue to prevent health coverage losses for Californians and stabilize the state’s health care system, and could provide additional support for nutrition assistance — which is also impacted by federal cuts — and for public education. Because the revenues would be one-time, the state would not be able to maintain these services in the future unless federal funding were fully restored or the state adopted alternative sources to raise this magnitude of revenue.
There is a strong rationale for taxing accumulated wealth — or taxing increases in wealth that currently go untaxed — given the profound wealth inequality and the vast unmet needs that exist in the state and across the country, as well as the ability of some ultrawealthy households to pay very little in income taxes as a share of their wealth.
At the same time, taxing wealth at the state level comes with some risks, particularly the potential for wealthy people to leave the state to avoid the tax, which would result in future state income tax losses if they did not return — putting at risk future funding for critical state services — and potential unknown impacts on the state economy. Prop. 40 attempts to counter that risk by applying the tax to billionaires who were California residents at the beginning of 2026, however it is likely this will be challenged in courts and the outcome is not certain.
In November, California voters will need to weigh the potential benefits of Prop. 40 against its potential tradeoffs.
Who Would Be Subject to the Tax Under Prop. 40 and How Would It Be Calculated?
Prop. 40 would institute a one-time tax on the worldwide wealth of billionaires. For the purposes of the measure, a billionaire subject to the tax could be an individual, a married couple, or a trust with net worth — as defined by the measure — above $1 billion. There are around250 billionaires in California, with over $2 trillion in total wealth (https://cabillionairetracker.org/). 1 (javascript:void(0)) Forbes tracks the daily wealth of billionaires with its “Real-Time Billionaires” list, and the California-specific data was compiled in connection with Jasper Boll, Emmanuel Saez, and Gabriel Zucman, California Billionaires: Wealth, Taxes, and Wealth Tax Revenue Estimates (https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/BSZ26CAbillionaires.pdf) (NBER Working Paper 35218, May 2026). Note: Saez is an author of Prop. 40.
The tax rate would be 5% for most billionaires, but the rate would be phased in for those with net worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion. 2 (javascript:void(0)) Specifically, the 5% rate would be reduced by 0.1 percentage point for each $2 million that the household’s net worth falls below $1.1 billion. Taxpayers would have the option of paying the full amount of the tax with their 2026 tax returns or in installments across five years, with an annual deferral charge.
Net worth is typically calculated as the total value of assets held by an individual, couple, or family minus their total debts. However, Prop. 40 allows some exclusions from the net worth calculation, including:
Real property holdings, which are subject to constitutional tax limitations due to Proposition 13, approved by California voters in 1978;
Tangible personal property — such as vehicles, jewelry, appliances, or business equipment — held outside of California; 3 (javascript:void(0)) Tangible personal property is excluded from the net worth calculation if it is held outside of California for at least 270 days during 2026 unless it was temporarily relocated for the purpose of tax avoidance. and
Certain pensions, retirement accounts, and deferred compensation arrangements.
The measure would apply the tax to billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026, and the amounts subject to the tax would be determined based on their net worth on December 31, 2026. There will likely be legal challenges to the application of the tax based on residency prior to the enactment of the tax. Federal and state tax measures often have retroactivity provisions to minimize tax avoidance and courts have upheld many of these laws, although it is unknown how courts would ultimately rule on this measure. The measure specifies that in the case the residency and valuation dates are invalidated by courts, these dates shall be construed to be the earliest dates consistent with law.
Prop. 40 establishes procedures for estimating the value of various types of assets that would be included in net worth for the purpose of the tax. Valuation is simple for some assets, such as holdings of publicly traded stock, which have a known market value at any given time. Other assets, such as shares of private businesses, intellectual property such as copyrights or trademarks, and artwork, are more difficult to value without a sale taking place. The measure has detailed valuation rules and formulas for different types of assets, and both the taxpayer and the state’s Franchise Tax Board — which would be responsible for administering the tax — could obtain certified appraisals in the case of valuation disputes. Additionally, the measure contains provisions intended to minimize the ability of taxpayers to avoid or evade their tax responsibility. 4 (javascript:void(0)) Tax avoidance reflects legal avenues to reducing tax liability, such as redirecting wealth holdings to exempted assets or relocating, whereas tax evasion encompasses illegal tactics to avoid taxes, such as hiding assets in tax havens, underreporting of asset values, or falsely claiming residency outside of the tax jurisdiction.
Example: Potential Impact of Prop. 40 on Mark Zuckerberg
Mark Zuckerberg, cofounder of Facebook, has a net worth of around $200 billion (https://www.forbes.com/profile/mark-zuckerberg/?ctpv=rtb&list=rtb). Assuming he has approximately $200 billion in wealth subject to Prop. 40 on December 31, 2026, when net worth is to be determined for the purpose of the measure, he would owe around $10 billion in tax, which he could pay in five annual installments of $2 billion. His remaining wealth of around $190 billion would still be more than the entire economies of dozens of countries, roughly on par with (https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.CD?most_recent_value_desc=true) the Gross Domestic Product of Morocco.
For comparison, Zuckerberg’s net worth increased 175% from 2023 to 2024 (https://www.forbes.com/profile/mark-zuckerberg/?ctpv=rtb&list=rtb) according to Forbes data, from $64.4 billion to $177 billion.
What Is the Difference Between Income and Wealth?
Capital Gains: Increases in Wealth
Households holding assets that have increased in value pay federal and state tax on those gains only when they sell those assets. This is known as a realized capital gain.
However, the value of an asset can grow exponentially and go untaxed as long as it is held onto — an unrealized capital gain. While the household doesn’t directly receive the proceeds from the gain until selling the asset, unrealized capital gains represent an increase in the household’s wealth and financial well-being (https://www.cbpp.org/research/federal-tax/arguments-against-taxing-unrealized-capital-gains-of-very-wealthy-fall-flat).
For ultra-wealthy households, unrealized capital gains make up a large share of their total wealth. 5 (javascript:void(0)) For example, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy estimated (https://itep.org/the-geographic-distribution-of-extreme-wealth-in-the-u-s/#:~:text=This%20ratio%20increases%20at%20higher%20levels%20of%20wealth%2C%20with%20unrealized%20gains%20making%20up%20almost%2070%20percent%20of%20billionaire%20wealth.) that unrealized capital gains represent nearly 70% of total wealth for billionaires. In some cases, ultra-wealthy households — such as corporate founders — can avoid paying income taxes entirely in some years by not taking a salary, not selling any stocks or other assets, and simply borrowing against their wealth to pay their bills. There is evidence of some of the wealthiest Americans engaging in this behavior, detailed in analyses of leaked tax returns by investigative journalists (https://www.propublica.org/article/the-secret-irs-files-trove-of-never-before-seen-records-reveal-how-the-wealthiest-avoid-income-tax), although recent research suggests (https://taxpolicycenter.org/taxvox/richs-real-tax-trick-isnt-buy-borrow-die) that this is not a widespread phenomenon and that overall, wealthy households do have significant taxable income and their incomes allow them to cover their expenses while continuing to invest and grow their wealth.
Additionally, if someone holds onto assets until their death, their heirs do not have to pay any tax on the gain due to a provision in both federal and state law known as “stepped-up basis (https://www.pgpf.org/article/what-is-the-stepped-up-basis-and-how-does-it-affect-the-federal-budget/),” estimated to cost California around $5 billion each year. 6 (javascript:void(0)) Department of Finance, Tax Expenditure Report: 2025-26 (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/forecasting/revenue-and-taxation/tax-expenditure-reports/2025-26-Tax-Expenditure-Report.pdf), p. 24. Note that the estimated annual cost of the provision is not equivalent to the revenue that could be generated from repealing it, and for this provision the revenue gains from repeal would start in the low hundreds of millions (https://lao.ca.gov/LAOEconTax/Article/Detail/797#:~:text=Eliminate%20Capital%20Gains%20Step%2DUp%20Basis%20on%20Inherited%20Assets.) and increase with time, potentially reaching $5 billion annually in the future. Essentially, the combination of unrealized capital gains not being taxed and stepped-up basis results in some large wealth increases never being taxed.
How Is Wealth Distributed Across California?
Across the country, the gaps in income (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/scf/dataviz/scf/chart/#range:1989,2022;series:Before_Tax_Income;demographic:inccat;population:all;units:median) and wealth (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/scf/dataviz/scf/chart/#range:1989,2022;series:Net_Worth;demographic:nwcat;population:all;units:median) have steadily grown with the top 10% of households seeing substantial growth in both income and wealth accumulation. Similarly, in California, only a tiny fraction of the population benefits from extreme income and wealth.
While both wealth and income inequality are prevalent in the state, wealth is even more unequally distributed (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/#:~:text=%C2%A0This%20difference%20is%20higher%20than%20in%20the%20rest%20of%20the%20country%2C%20where%20the%2080th%20percentile%20is%2099%20times%20the%2020th%2C%20and%20higher%20than%20income%20inequality%20in%20California.) than income in California. While the state has more wealth than the rest of the country (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/), the disparities in wealth are also starkest in California.
When focusing on the wealth distribution in the state, the data show an alarming gap between households with high and low wealth. Specifically, the wealthiest 20% of households have a net worth of over $1.5 million (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/#:~:text=High%20net%20worth%20households%20have%20substantially%20more%20wealth%20than%20low%20net%20worth%20households.), while the bottom 20% of households have a net worth of $13,000 or less. Those who would be subject to the Prop. 40 tax — those with a net worth above $1 billion — have a net worth of over 3,000 times the median household.
Wealth is also unequally distributed across racial and ethnic groups. For example, the median net worth of white households in 2023 was almost ten times (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/#:~:text=Net%20worth%20is%20highest%20among%20older%2C%20college%2Deducated%2C%20and%20white%20and%20Asian%20households.) the median net worth of Latinx households, reflecting the historical barriers to wealth accumulation (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/) these communities have faced. Black, Latinx, and other households of color often have less wealth due to many factors including a lower likelihood of owning stocks (https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/03/06/a-booming-us-stock-market-doesnt-benefit-all-racial-and-ethnic-groups-equally/), occupational segregation (https://www.americanprogress.org/article/occupational-segregation-in-america/) pushing them into lower-payer jobs, and a lack of inherited generational wealth (https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/p/2021-12-17-inheritances-by-race/). These factors likely contribute to the large wealth disparities that have persisted throughout history.
How Much Revenue Will Prop. 40 Raise?
There is a high degree of uncertainty in estimating the potential revenue from this measure since it is impossible to accurately predict how billionaires and the courts will respond to the tax. It is likely there will be some avoidance and evasion of the tax, as billionaires may hide or underreport their assets, shift their asset holdings toward those that are exempt from the tax, attempt to sever their ties with California, or engage in other tactics to minimize or eliminate their tax liability.
After attempting to account for these factors, the Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) that the billionaire tax would likely raise “tens of billions” of dollars in the near term. Empowering State and Local Governance
This paper examines the revenue and migration impact of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act, a one-time 5 percent tax on the worldwide net worth of individuals exceeding $1 billion. Using data from the Forbes Billionaire List, news reports detailing the residential real estate holdings of California billionaires, and public announcements of billionaire departures from the state, we estimate the behavioral response and associated revenue loss to this new tax using several different methodologies. Even before accounting for reductions in other tax bases such as the income tax, we estimate that the Act will collect approximately $30 billion (range $28 to 36 billion), less than a third of the $100 billion projected by Galle et al. (2025). This range accounts for the publicly confirmed taxpayer migration that has already eliminated nearly 30 percent of the Act's wealth tax base, applies a litigation-survival discount to the remaining base, and is validated by the wealth tax base elasticity literature. We estimate that California's billionaires contribute $3.3–5.8 billion annually in state income taxes. The present value of permanently lost income tax collections from departures more than offsets the one-time wealth tax revenue, yielding a net present value of negative $38.9 billion. Across 100,000 simulated revenue and discount rate combinations, 85 percent of plausible outcomes produce a negative net present value of state revenues.
See this Liberty Lens essay (https://libertylensecon.substack.com/p/california-wealth-tax-npv) for a summary of the paper's findings.
